5.text: In the ceremonial described (Plate XXXII, Fig. 4) all those present, down

6.text: to the very small children, have to perform some exercise on the drum;

7.text: while the women and the younger boys appear in turn as dancers. Then a

8.text: feast follows, in which the men eat freely of the raw meat of walrus-heads,

9.text: slicing it off with their knives. The ivory of the walrus and the remainder

10.text: of the meat are divided among all the members of the crew, in accordance

11.text: with the usual rules, which will be spoken of in the third part of this work.

12.text: At the end of the ceremonial, all of the participants, particularly the

13.text: women and children, shake off, over the big lamp, all diseases to which they

14.text: may be liable, and, in general, their bad luck. The lamp, however, is covered

15.text: with a wooden plank to protect the fire from contamination. The particles

16.text: of rubbish, and especially the hair which has fallen from the fur clothes down

17.text: on the plank, are picked up and burned, together with the plank, in a

18.text: separate fire. The ashes of the fire are afterward carefully collected, and

19.text: carried out of the house to be left in the wilderness. The bones and crumbs

20.text: of the feast are gathered up and thrown into the sea to send back the

24.text: sacrifice thrown into a small fire built up before the entrance of the tent.

29.text: Chukchee. The sacrifice to Pehiˊttin has no features peculiar to the Maritime

31.text: Ceremonial of Antlers. — The ceremony of antlers (kiˊlvei) is performed

32.text: with boughs, which are gathered in a heap on the place of sacrifice, behind

33.text: the house. Then a fire is arranged and sacrificed to with tallow or meat.

34.text: Those who have a few reindeer, with some reindeer-breeding friend, take care

35.text: to have a few antlers on the top of their heap of boughs. Only those

36.text: Asiatic Eskimo who have succeeded in acquiring reindeer-herds² celebrate this

37.text: ceremonial. These, as remarked before, consider themselves obliged to per-

38.text: form all the ceremonials connected with reindeer-breeding life; at least, to the

39.text: same extent as do their neighbors of Maritime Chukchee origin.
